h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: Edge 0 none cuts node 1 off from the input so edge 2 is disconnected and its usually positive upgrade shrinks toward zero.
With edge 0 none, node 1 carries no signal so edge 4 is disconnected and its usual gain from conv3x3 vanishes.
Removing an already disconnected edge costs nothing, so the usually negative effect of none shrinks toward zero.
Edge 4 is fed only by dead node 1, so deleting it changes nothing and the usual loss disappears.
Replacing an empty bypass with a strong conv adds a whole new path, a larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Replacing none on the sole input edge of node 1 restores the whole branch, giving a far larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Replacing the strongest op with an identity on the stem of the deep path loses the most, so the usual negative effect is amplified.
Deleting a conv3x3 removes the most valuable op, a larger loss than deleting a weak pool or skip.
Deleting a conv3x3 on the direct input-to-output edge loses a strong path, a bigger drop than deleting a weak op or an already empty edge.
Cutting a conv3x3 stem on edge 0 also disables edges 2 and 4, so the loss is much larger than when edge 0 held a weak op.
